Health & Recovery

Sleep and muscle growth: why your gains depend on it

Lifters will track every gram of protein and then sleep six hours a night. Sleep is when much of your recovery happens, and cutting it short quietly undermines your strength, your muscle gains and your fat loss.

By the FormFit Editorial Team · Reviewed October 2026 · 5 min read

How much sleep you need

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society recommend that adults get 7 or more hours a night regularly. Most people who train hard do best with 7 to 9 hours; teenagers need more, about 8 to 10.

Time in bed is not the same as time asleep. If you are in bed for 7 hours, you might sleep only 6 to 6.5. Plan for 7.5 to 8.5 hours in bed to get 7 to 8 hours of actual sleep.

What happens to muscle while you sleep

Several recovery processes peak at night. A large share of daily growth hormone is released during deep sleep, and testosterone levels in men are closely tied to sleep, rising through the night.

Sleep loss shifts hormones the wrong way: less testosterone and more cortisol, which favours breakdown over building. In one study, a single night without sleep reduced muscle protein synthesis by about 18 percent in young adults (Lamon et al., Physiological Reports, 2021).

Most research uses severe or total sleep loss, so the effect of losing an hour or two is smaller. But chronic short sleep adds up over months of training.

Sleep, strength and performance

Short sleep tends to reduce performance on long or repeated efforts and make the same weight feel harder. Single maximal lifts often hold up after one bad night, but volume, motivation and focus suffer.

Reaction time and coordination also drop, which matters for complex lifts like squats and deadlifts and raises injury risk. Several studies of athletes link sleeping under about 7 hours with higher injury rates.

After a very poor night, keep the session but drop the top sets. Do your warm-ups, work at moderate weights, and save heavy attempts for a day you have slept.

Sleep and fat loss

Sleep may matter most when you are dieting. In a well-known study (Nedeltcheva et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2010), people on the same calorie deficit lost similar weight whether they slept 5.5 or 8.5 hours, but the short sleepers lost about 55 percent less of that weight as fat and more as lean mass.

Short sleep also increases hunger. Levels of ghrelin, the hunger hormone, tend to rise, while leptin, which signals fullness, drops. Most people eat more and crave higher-calorie food after a bad night, making a deficit harder to hold.

If you are cutting, protecting sleep is one of the easiest ways to keep more muscle. Pair it with the targets from the weight loss calculator and a high protein intake.

Practical steps to sleep better

  1. Fix your wake time. Get up at the same time every day, including weekends, within about an hour. It anchors your body clock more than bedtime does.
  2. Get daylight early. 10 to 20 minutes outside in the morning helps set your rhythm.
  3. Cut caffeine by mid-afternoon. Caffeine's effects can last six hours or more. That includes pre-workout drinks.
  4. Keep the room cool, dark and quiet. Around 16 to 19 °C (60 to 67 °F) suits most people.
  5. Wind down for 30 to 60 minutes. Dim lights, put work away, and keep the phone out of bed.
  6. Limit alcohol. It helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep in the second half of the night.
  7. Do not go to bed stuffed or starving. A moderate meal two to three hours before bed works for most.

Training late without wrecking sleep

Evening training is fine for most people. Studies suggest exercise ending at least an hour before bed generally does not harm sleep. Very hard sessions close to bedtime can leave some people wired.

If you train late, skip stimulant pre-workouts, keep the last hour of the evening calm and take a warm shower, which helps your body cool down afterwards.

Pre-sleep protein

Eating protein before bed can support overnight muscle protein synthesis. A study by Res et al. (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, 2012) found that 40 g of casein protein taken before sleep after evening training increased overnight muscle protein synthesis.

This matters most if your evening meal was early or protein-light. Good options include milk, Greek yoghurt, curd, cottage cheese or paneer, all rich in slow-digesting casein. Your daily total, set with the protein calculator, still matters most. More on timing in pre and post workout nutrition.

Tracking your sleep

Wearables and phone apps estimate sleep from movement and heart rate. They are reasonably good at total sleep time and poor at telling sleep stages apart, so treat deep sleep and REM figures as rough guesses.

The most useful things to track are simple: what time you went to bed, what time you got up, and how rested you felt on a scale of 1 to 5. Put a column for it next to your training log, and you will quickly see how your sessions track your sleep.

Do not let tracking itself keep you awake. If checking your sleep score makes you anxious, take the watch off for a week and go by how you feel.

Early training, shift work and busy schedules

If you lift at 5 or 6 in the morning, the time has to come from somewhere. Move bedtime earlier rather than cutting sleep; training at 5:30 on five hours of sleep is often worse than training at 6:30 on seven.

Shift workers face a harder problem, because the body clock resists changing. A few things help:

  • Keep the same sleep window on work days where you can, even if it is during the day.
  • Make the bedroom fully dark with blackout curtains or an eye mask, and use earplugs.
  • Wear sunglasses on the way home from a night shift to limit morning light.
  • Schedule hard sessions after your main sleep, not before.

When sleep is limited for a stretch, such as a newborn or exam season, cut training volume rather than skipping sleep to keep it. Shorter sessions focused on the main lifts will hold most of your strength.

Supplements, naps and catching up

Most sleep supplements have weak evidence for healthy adults, and none fixes poor habits.

SupplementWhat the evidence suggests
MelatoninUseful for jet lag and shifting your body clock; small effect on general sleep. Prescription-only in some countries
MagnesiumMay help if you are deficient; limited evidence otherwise
Glycine, L-theanineSmall studies, modest effects
Antihistamine sleep aidsCan cause next-day grogginess; not for regular use

Check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking any sleep aid, particularly if you take other medication, are pregnant, or have a health condition. Persistent insomnia is best treated with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which has strong evidence.

A 20 to 30 minute nap in the early afternoon can restore alertness and help performance after a short night. Longer naps or naps late in the day can make it harder to fall asleep at night.

Sleeping in at weekends partly offsets a short week but shifts your body clock, making Monday harder. Steady sleep beats catching up.

If you have had a run of bad nights, focus on getting back to your normal wake time rather than lying in. One or two early nights are usually enough to reset.

If you regularly snore loudly, wake gasping, or feel exhausted despite enough time in bed, talk to a doctor. Sleep apnoea is common, especially in larger and heavier lifters, and very treatable. Read more about recovery in rest days and recovery.

Frequently asked questions

Can you build muscle on 6 hours of sleep?

You can still build muscle, but likely more slowly, with less energy for training and more muscle loss when dieting. Most people who train hard do better with 7 to 9 hours.

Do muscles grow while you sleep?

Muscle repair and growth happen around the clock, but several key processes peak during sleep, including growth hormone release. Poor sleep reduces muscle protein synthesis and recovery.

Is it better to sleep or work out if I am tired?

After one poor night, a lighter session is usually fine. If you are chronically short of sleep, an extra hour of sleep will do more for your progress than an extra session.

Should I eat before bed to build muscle?

A protein-rich snack before bed, such as milk, yoghurt or cottage cheese, can support overnight recovery, especially if your last meal was early. Total daily protein matters more.

General information for healthy adults, not medical advice. See our medical disclaimer.
